children: By Steve Garmhausen
The next differentiator for wealth management firms serving high-net-worth families might not be tax services or concierge perks-it could be helping them live healthier lives.

RWA Wealth Partners, for example, refers clients to a healthcare advisory business in its network that guides families through healthcare and longevity decisions. "Having those types of partners has been powerful for us," says Michelle Knight, CEO and chief economist of the Boston-based wealth firm, which ranks No. 32 in Barron's 2026 Top 100 RIA Firms list. "It has been a gift to be able to offer that to people."

Knight and Joseph "JP" Powers, the firm's chief investment officer, spoke with Barron's Advisor about the investment opportunities in artificial intelligence, RWA's origins inside law firm Ropes & Gray, and how the advisory's structure facilitates its goal of serving clients through the stages of their financial life. An edited version of the conversation follows.
Barron's: Let's start with investing. What's the bond market telling us with its rising long-term yields?

Joseph Powers: As we talk today, the U.S. has crossed $40 trillion of debt. I would characterize economic growth as solid but not impressive, and inflation is still running well above target. It isn't a sustainable trend. And it has been compounded recently by the high issuance of debt by companies tied to the artificial-intelligence buildout. The sheer scale of that issuance has pulled yields higher. We've had some Treasury interventions this month aimed at trying to keep a cap on yields. But we've felt that it's also going to take action from the Federal Reserve to move the needle, just because of the sheer size of their balance sheet.

I think the issue the market has had is that this new regime has been reluctant to provide any forward guidance. There were some signs from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's [recent] speech that he's leaning in that direction. I think he does want to be hawkish on inflation; that's his track record. But he also has to navigate a relationship with the White House. I think we're still going through this adjustment period and feeling out how he's going to communicate, but the market's starting to figure out what those signals will be.
Where are you seeing the best opportunities in the stock market?

Powers: I would call this a middling economy right now, if we were just looking at pure economic growth and the strength of the labor market. I wouldn't characterize it as overly impressive by historical standards, certainly when adjusted for inflation. But the strength of the equity markets and of corporate earnings has been impressive, and that's where we operate for most clients.

While there is a lot to be concerned about geopolitically or even economically, if we look at how businesses are doing, it is hard to argue with the results. A lot of that is, of course, tied to the buildout of AI infrastructure, which has added a tremendous amount of capital investment globally. It has given equity investors something to stay excited about.

As far as opportunities to invest new dollars from here, I think it will be the services that will run on these AI platforms that can add real value for businesses and consumers for years to come. Those are the types of opportunities we're most interested in right now. They could do well even if the global macro environment isn't firing on all cylinders for the next several quarters or even couple of years.
Is it too soon to bet on specific companies?

Powers: It's hard to pick the eventual winners and losers. But I might use the software space as an example. That market has been steamrolled this year, with the incumbent software companies left for dead, largely feeling like they're going to be replaced by AI. It was nice to get some early results from firms like Salesforce, which were able to say, "Look, we're going to be able to use these AI tools to our own benefit, and don't forget about us." And all of a sudden, that stock is being rewarded.
Let's turn to your firm. How did RWA Wealth Partners come together?

Michelle Knight: RWA Wealth Partners came from the combination of Advisor Investments and Ropes Wealth Advisors in mid-2023. I was the leader of Ropes Wealth Advisors, which had been wholly owned by law firm Ropes & Gray; we rebranded later that year. We are employee owned, with private-equity backing from Summit Partners, which is also Boston-based.
Who are your target clients, and what do you do for them?

Knight: One of the things we talked about before putting the two companies together that was so exciting was this idea that we could have a firm where clients could be served at every stage of their financial life. So, whether a client was accumulating wealth-working hard and saving money, taking care of their family, and thinking about retirement in the future-or having significant liquidity events like inheritance or the sale of a business, all the way through to legacy and wealth-transfer planning, the idea was to provide a team with a lot of experience and skills serving clients at those different stages.
So, we built two divisions within the company, one for private wealth and one for family office, and we have recruited and enhanced our team to have the skills to meet clients where they are.
Why did Ropes & Gray part with its wealth management business?

Knight: I was part of the team that set up the registered investment advisor for Ropes & Gray back in 2014. We opened our doors in 2015, formalizing what had been a trust and estates offering that dated to the founding of Ropes & Gray in 1865.

We grew into one of the top 10 RIA firms in New England, and we had big plans for our future. We wanted employee ownership. We wanted to think about a national service model. So we decided, together with Ropes & Gray, to spin out. We joined forces with another firm, Advisor Investments, which was right in our backyard, in Newton, Mass. I actually learned to drive in the parking lot of their offices, so it felt very familiar to me. I knew a lot of the advisors who worked there, and it felt like the two firms were thinking through how we wanted to grow.
Do you continue to have a client-referral relationship with Ropes & Gray?

Knight: We sure do, and as you can imagine, we've expanded our relationships with other law firms around the country that might have been reluctant to work with us when we were wholly owned by Ropes & Gray. We uniquely understand the needs of law firm partners themselves as successful professionals, and often their clients who are experiencing transactions and successful careers.
What's it like to be an RWA advisor? I would imagine the culture is somewhat buttoned-up, having sprouted out of a law firm.

Powers: That's a fair assessment. As well as being CIO, I'm also an advisor. I think Michelle has created a great team-oriented environment here, and led from the top. I think that that approach resonates with clients. When we get together with them, they're typically in front of a full team rather than working with a single individual who's supposed to have all the answers to every question that comes up. We think this approach works better for clients, but also contributes to why we've been able to attract and retain such great people over the years.
One of the services you provide is connecting clients with healthcare advisors. Can you describe that?

Knight: We care about our clients and want to think about how we can help them marshal resources in times of great stress. So, we have developed a business relationship with a healthcare advisory firm. We might refer clients to them in an emergency moment or if it's more of just thinking through changes in memory or living in a supported community. Having those types of partners has been powerful for us. It has been a gift to be able to offer that to people.
I've definitely seen more advisory firms venturing into the healthcare space, usually through partnerships.

Knight: Yes, and it's authentic to us. Some firms focus more on concierge services like aviation. We're probably more focused on health and longevity. And our clientele is multigenerational, so we like to help people within families take care of each other. That's more on brand for us.
Advisory fee models are evolving. What's your approach when you provide a range of services?

Knight: We really do want to offer comprehensive wealth management, and we want our clients to feel like they get a lot of value. Every client receives financial planning, investment management, tax planning, and estate planning strategies. That's all part of our standard fee structure. When we take a step further and are doing things like tax compliance, we typically charge flat fees. There can be situations where we will consider an hourly rate. But we typically charge flat annual fees for services like tax compliance, estate settlement, certain types of consulting services or engagements, and project-based work.
How much of your growth strategy is adding one client at a time versus buying other firms?

Knight: We're primarily focused on organic growth. We have had some successful mergers and acquisitions and lift-outs in the past 18 months, which we're proud of. But when you do a great job for clients, they tell their friends, they tell their family, they tell their neighbors. That's our best sales strategy, and we've been fortunate to be able to grow in that way.
What is RWA's "Wealth With Intention" initiative?

Knight: That is like my beating heart. Jennifer Votano and Evelyn Pepe joined RWA last year to spearhead this initiative about educating, engaging, and empowering women and rising generations. We are doing this through education, with events, tools, and resources. It's about having a community and great conversations.

With every event we have, every dinner we host, every speaker we bring to the table, I feel so much pride that I'm running a firm that prioritizes and invests in this. Clients and the team love it. It takes a lot of work and a lot of resources to make those things happen and to build that community, but it just lights up and energizes a culture.
How do you walk the line between supporting your advisors and clients and keeping your private-equity partner happy?

Knight: What's exciting about having a partner like Summit Partners is they're a growth-oriented PE firm. Their focus is to support us in our growth plans and trajectory. Think about an athlete: How do you make them run faster and have more endurance?

Since I took leadership of the company, my dialogue with them and our full board has been relentlessly about our service and sales culture. It has been about how recruitment and retention of talent is the best growth strategy. It has been about how we can be in places where we can serve. How do we invest in things like Wealth With Intention that may not have an immediate return on investment but have an enormous spiritual ROI that comes from creating a community, not only for clients but also for employees?

In addition, I'm an advisor, as is JP, and that brings a unique perspective. When our leadership team speaks to our board we're thinking about the strategy of the business and their interests, but we also have boots on the ground. On a personal note, I'm one of the only women leaders of a large wealth management firm in the country, and I have never felt a moment where I haven't felt full support. I have the incredible privilege of being in this position at a time when wealth is transferring in vast amounts to women stakeholders.
Thanks, Michelle and JP.
